intro.title: Implement KeysMatching type
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom TypeScript utility type called `KeysMatching`. This type will filter the keys of an object to only include those whose values match a specified type. The core concept involves using mapped types and conditional types to iterate over object keys and check their value types. You will work with keyof, extends, and indexed access types to implement this logic. By the end, you will understand how to create reusable type utilities that enhance type safety in your TypeScript projects.
intro.usecase: The `KeysMatching` type is essential for building type-safe data filtering and selection components in real-world applications. For example, in a product dashboard with a dynamic filter panel, you need to ensure that a user can only select filter keys that correspond to numeric columns (like 'price' or 'inventory') for a range slider, not text-based ones. This pattern allows TypeScript to enforce that a 'filterByNumericKey' prop can only accept keys of the data object whose values are numbers, preventing runtime errors. It's commonly used in component libraries for tables, advanced search interfaces, and configuration panels where UI controls must be dynamically bound to specific, type-appropriate properties of a data model.

objectives: Construct a generic type that filters object keys based on value type
Apply conditional types to evaluate type compatibility within mapped types
Implement the KeysMatching type using key remapping and type inference
Manipulate union types to extract matching keys from object structures
Integrate the KeysMatching type with existing TypeScript interfaces
Configure type constraints to ensure type safety during key extraction
Render type-safe functions that accept only specific property keys

steps.instruction: Add a comment below the interface explaining what KeysMatching should do: extract keys whose values match a given type.

steps.title: Start implementing KeysMatching type
steps.instruction: Define the KeysMatching type with two generic parameters: T (object type) and U (value type to match). Use the 'type' keyword to create this generic type.
steps.hint: Start with 'type KeysMatching<T, U> = ' followed by the type definition. You'll fill in the actual logic in later steps.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: generic type with two parameters
type Pair<A, B> = [A, B];
steps.expectedOutcome: A generic type named KeysMatching with two type parameters T and U is defined, ready for implementation.
successCriteria: The KeysMatching type is defined with two generic parameters T and U using the 'type' keyword.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the 'type' keyword and have both T and U as generic parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The KeysMatching type definition is missing or incorrect. It should start with 'type KeysMatching<T, U> = '.

steps.title: Use keyof operator to get object keys
steps.instruction: Inside the KeysMatching type definition, apply the keyof operator to T to get a union of all its keys.
steps.hint: Use keyof T to extract all property names from type T as a union type.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: extracting keys from an interface
type PersonKeys = keyof Person; // 'name' | 'age' | 'email'
steps.expectedOutcome: The KeysMatching type now uses keyof to extract all keys from type T as a union type.
successCriteria: The KeysMatching type definition includes keyof T.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using keyof T inside the KeysMatching type definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: The KeysMatching type should use keyof T to extract all keys from type T.

steps.title: Filter keys using conditional types
steps.instruction: Update the KeysMatching type to use a mapped type with a conditional check: for each key K in keyof T, check if T[K] extends U, and if so, keep K.
steps.hint: Use the syntax: [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends U ? K : never. This creates a mapped type where each key either maps to itself (if the value type matches U) or to never.
steps.expectedOutcome: The KeysMatching type now uses a mapped type with a conditional check to filter keys based on their value type.
successCriteria: The KeysMatching type is updated to use a mapped type with a conditional check: [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends U ? K : never.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct conditional type syntax: T[K] extends U ? K : never.
steps.feedbackWrong: The KeysMatching type should use a mapped type with a conditional check. Try: [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends U ? K : never.

steps.title: Extract matching keys with indexed access
steps.instruction: Update the KeysMatching type to use indexed access with the conditional type to extract only the keys where T[K] extends U.
steps.hint: After the conditional check, use the key K in the true branch of the conditional type to collect the matching keys.
steps.expectedOutcome: The KeysMatching type should now properly filter keys using conditional types and indexed access to produce a union of keys where the property type matches U.
successCriteria: The KeysMatching type uses a mapped type with a conditional check and indexed access to extract matching keys.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your conditional type returns K for matching keys and never for non-matching ones, then use indexed access with [keyof T].
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's review: The KeysMatching type needs to map over keys, check if T[K] extends U, return K for matches, and use indexed access to get the union of matching keys.
